summary: Describes a mechanism for providing cryptographic authentication for IPv4 and IPv6 datagrams. It is the original Authentication Header specification, later replaced by RFC 2402.

eli5.summary: A signature stamped on each Internet packet that shows who sent it and that no one changed it.

questions: what is the ip authentication header
how does ah authenticate ip packets
how does authentication work in ip
subtitle: Cryptographic authentication to verify IP datagrams came from who they claim and haven't been altered in transit.

tldr.problem: The Internet Protocol does not verify the source of a datagram or detect if it has been modified in transit, making networks vulnerable to spoofed and forged packets.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Header provides a cryptographic signature computed over the entire datagram using a key shared between sender and receiver. The signature is carried in a new header inserted after the IP header.
tldr.outcome: IP datagrams can now be authenticated end-to-end, ensuring they came from the claimed source and were not altered. This RFC was later superseded by RFC 2402, which integrated it into the IPsec architecture.

today: RFC 1826 is a historic Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 2402, which provides the same authentication functionality as part of the IPsec protocol suite. Modern IPsec implementations use RFC 2402 and its successors. RFC 1826 remains important for understanding the history of IPsec authentication mechanisms.

sections.title: Authentication for IP Datagrams
sections.content:
The IP Authentication Header (AH) is a mechanism for providing cryptographic authentication to IP datagrams. It computes a signature called Authentication Data over the entire datagram using a shared secret key, then inserts a new header carrying this signature immediately after the IP header.

Unlike simple checksums that can be easily forged, AH uses cryptographically strong algorithms that make it computationally infeasible to modify a datagram and recalculate a valid signature without the shared key. This provides both integrity protection (proving the datagram was not modified) and source authentication (proving who sent it), depending on the algorithm and key management used.

The RFC distinguishes AH from the IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), which provides confidentiality by encrypting the datagram contents. AH does not hide data; it only authenticates it. Users who need both authentication and encryption should use ESP or combine it with AH.
sections.eli5: When you mail a check, the bank needs proof it actually came from you and not a forger. AH is like a signature stamp on the check that the bank can verify matches your account without someone else being able to fake it.

sections.title: The Authentication Header Structure
sections.content:
The AH is a simple fixed-format header inserted between the IP header and the data being authenticated. For IPv4, it comes right after the IP header. For IPv6, it normally comes after the hop-by-hop and routing headers, before encryption (if used).

The header contains four fields. The Next Header field (8 bits) indicates what comes after the AH, using the same protocol numbers as the IP header (for example, 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP). The Length field (8 bits) specifies the size of the Authentication Data in 32-bit words. A 16-bit Reserved field is set to zero and included in the authentication calculation for alignment. The Security Parameters Index (SPI) is a 32-bit value that identifies the security association—the shared key and algorithm pair used between sender and receiver.

The Authentication Data field is variable-length and contains the cryptographic signature. The signature is calculated by the sender over the entire packet and verified by the receiver; for authentication purposes, the Authentication Data field itself is treated as all zeros during the calculation, preventing circular dependencies.
sections.eli5: The header is a small label with four pieces of information: what comes next, how long the signature is, a magic number identifying which shared secret to use, and the actual signature stamp itself.

sections.title: How Authentication Works
sections.content:
Before sending a packet, the sender looks up the Security Association (SA) based on the destination address and the user or application sending the packet. The SA is a table entry maintained by key management software that specifies which cryptographic algorithm to use, the shared key, and other parameters.

The sender then computes the signature over the datagram using the specified algorithm and key. Two special rules apply: fields that change in transit (like the IP Time-to-Live or Hop Limit) are set to zero for the calculation, since the receiver cannot predict their final value. When using IPv6, options marked with a specific flag are also zeroed out. The resulting signature is placed in the Authentication Data field, and the SPI value identifying the SA is inserted in the header.

On the receiving end, the recipient uses the destination address and SPI to locate the same SA, then independently recalculates the signature. If the recalculated signature matches the one in the Authentication Data field, the packet is accepted as authentic and unmodified. If it does not match, the packet is silently discarded and the failure is logged with details like the SPI, timestamp, source address, and destination address.
sections.eli5: Before mailing, you compute a unique seal based on the letter content and your secret key. When it arrives, the recipient recomputes the seal with the same secret and compares them. If they match, the letter is real. If they don't, someone tampered with it.

sections.title: Key Management and Security Associations
sections.content:
The RFC deliberately decouples the AH specification from key management, because key management protocols are notoriously error-prone. The only connection between the two is the Security Parameters Index, a simple 32-bit number that points to a pre-established Security Association.

A Security Association is unidirectional: one SA exists from host A to host B, and a separate SA exists for the reverse direction. Key management software (running separately) creates and maintains a table of SAs, each specifying the algorithm, key, padding requirements, and other parameters. Different users or applications can have different SAs to the same destination, allowing fine-grained control over which keying material is used.

The RFC requires that implementations support manual key distribution—pre-shared keys configured by an administrator—and must support keyed MD5 as the minimum algorithm. Other algorithms can be added, but keyed MD5 is the baseline for conformance. This separation allows key management to be upgraded or fixed without changing the AH implementation.
sections.eli5: A table keeps track of which shared secrets work for which directions and destinations. A separate program manages this table, allowing the authentication part to stay simple and the keys to be managed safely elsewhere.

sections.title: Security Strengths and Limitations
sections.content:
The security provided by AH depends entirely on four factors: the strength of the underlying cryptographic algorithm, the strength of the shared key, the correctness of the implementation, and the security of the key management system. If any of these is weak, the authentication is compromised. For example, if the algorithm is broken, the key is short, the code has a bug, or the key is stolen, the authentication fails.

AH authenticates the datagram contents but does not hide them from eavesdroppers. Users needing confidentiality must use encryption (ESP) instead of or in addition to AH. Similarly, AH does not protect against traffic analysis: an attacker can still see that packets are being exchanged, when, and in what volume.

One subtle issue arises with ICMP error messages: if a large authenticated packet triggers an ICMP error that gets truncated to fit in the minimum IP message size, the recipient may not be able to verify the truncated ICMP response, leading to a conflict between security (not trusting unauthenticated data) and robustness (reacting appropriately to legitimate errors). The RFC acknowledges this tension but offers no complete solution.
sections.eli5: The seal only works if your secret is really secret, the math is strong, and your software is bug-free. The seal proves the letter wasn't opened, but it doesn't hide what's inside, and a thief can still see you're exchanging letters.

fields.name: Next Header
fields.desc: IP protocol number of the next header (e.g., 6 for TCP, 17 for UDP).

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of Authentication Data in 32-bit words.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Set to zero; included in authentication calculation.

fields.name: Security Parameters Index
fields.desc: Identifies the security association and shared key to use.

fields.name: Authentication Data
fields.desc: Variable-length cryptographic signature over the entire datagram (shown: 128 bits for MD5).
